newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Boehler sees hard year ahead but steady dividend.
newsitem.headline: Boehler sees hard year ahead but steady dividend.

text.p: Austrian high-grade steelmaker Boehler-Uddeholm on Monday posted lower-than-expected first-half earnings but said it would strive to maintain its current three percent dividend level.
The company said it expected pre-tax earnings to remain in line with 1995, but warned net profit would be hard hit due to changes in Austria's tax laws.

"We believe we can keep pre-tax profit at the same high level as last year," chief executive Claus Raidl told a news conference. In 1995, Boehler reported pre-tax earnings of 1.351 billion schillings ($128.7 million) and paid a dividend of 25 schillings per share.
Pre-tax profit for the first half rose to 778.7 million schillings from 696.3 million a year earlier.
First-half net profit fell seven percent to 552.9 million schillings as the group's tax burden increased, and the company said it expected a further decline for the full year.
The group, which was privatised by the Austrian government last year, said the tax rate in the first six months of the year had risen to 29 percent from 14 percent a year ago.
Group sales inched up to 9.339 billion schillings from 9.221 billion.
"We are pleased to have been able to maintain a high level of profitability in spite of the relatively flat economy," Raidl said.

He predicted turnover would decline further due to the sale of non-core businesses and to a shift in the year-end balance of a joint venture with Germany's Thyssen, which meant 500 million schillings would not be included in this year's consolidated results.

Boehler said demand in its core European markets had been "relatively good", albeit with strong declines in Germany and Austria. American markets had been stable, while the Pacific Rim had shown a slight decrease, the group added.
While prices remained at the level of the first quarter, price pressures on its main markets had markedly increased, Boehler said.
Finance director Horst Koenigslehner forecast overall demand would decrease by around four percent in the second half, and prices by two percent.
The speciality-steel maker makes about 61 percent of its sales in European Union countries, with long-products accounting for almost two thirds of turnover.
The group said job cuts at its facilities in Austria and Sweden should help to counteract already noticeable weak order intake and backlog to maintain earnings at last year's levels.
Order intake fell 27 percent to 5,028 billion schillings, while orders on hand were down 32 percent at 3.135 billion.
"We are okay now structurally, but we have to coordinate our breathing with the economy," said Raidl.
"Our job is to be prepared in case 1997 is worse. Of course we hope it will be better than 1996," he added. ($ = 10.49 Austrian Schillings)
